summary: Describes a change to AS112 deployment that uses DNS DNAME records. With it, zones can be redirected to AS112 servers and removed again without every AS112 operator having to edit their own server configuration.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of every helper desk updating its own list, one forwarding sign at the main desk says to send these questions to the helper desk. Changing the sign is easy.

questions: how to add zone to as112
how to redirect a zone to as112
subtitle: How a single DNAME record lets any zone owner send junk queries to the AS112 sink without asking its operators.

tldr.problem: Sinking queries for private-use address zones at AS112 required delegating each zone to the AS112 nameservers, and loosely coordinated operators made adding or removing zones slow and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: A new zone, EMPTY.AS112.ARPA, is hosted on a new anycast nameserver, and any zone owner redirects a part of the namespace to it with a DNAME record.
tldr.outcome: Zones can be redirected to AS112 or released at any time without changes to AS112 nodes, and the existing delegations keep working unchanged.

today: RFC 7535 is an Informational document, published in May 2015, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Operational guidance for AS112 servers is in RFC 7534.

sections.title: The AS112 Problem
sections.content:
Many sites use IPv4 addresses that are not globally unique, such as the private-use addresses in RFC 1918. Devices there may send reverse lookup queries for those addresses, and such queries often leak into the public DNS where no server can answer them usefully. The volume is large and growing.

The AS112 project, named after its Autonomous System Number, provides a distributed sink for these queries to reduce the load on the IN-ADDR.ARPA authoritative servers. Its nameservers are PRISONER.IANA.ORG, BLACKHOLE-1.IANA.ORG and BLACKHOLE-2.IANA.ORG, and they must answer authoritatively for every zone delegated to them. Otherwise clients following referrals meet a lame delegation.

Because AS112 operators are only loosely coordinated and the servers are reached by anycast, adding or removing a zone accurately is hard, and so is testing remotely whether a node is configured for a given zone. Instead of delegating zones directly, this RFC uses DNAME redirection, defined in RFC 6672. The AS112 project itself is described in RFC 7534.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers keep asking questions that have no real answer. A special helper desk takes those questions, but changing what the desk handles used to be slow because many people had to agree.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.content:
A new zone, EMPTY.AS112.ARPA, is delegated to a single nameserver, BLACKHOLE.AS112.ARPA, with IPv4 address 192.31.196.1 and IPv6 address 2001:4:112::1. The addresses are chosen so that each is covered by a prefix (a /24 for IPv4 and a /48 for IPv6) in which no other address is used. That lets the service be spread by anycast using one IPv4 and one IPv6 service prefix.

Some or all existing AS112 nodes should be extended to support the new addresses and host the EMPTY.AS112.ARPA zone. Each part of the namespace whose queries should be sunk is then redirected to that zone with a DNAME record.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one new mailbox address for all the unanswerable questions. Anyone who wants their questions to go there just writes that address on a forwarding note.

sections.title: Operating and Redirecting
sections.content:
Operators of AS112 nodes configure the two new addresses, announce covering routes for them and host the EMPTY.AS112.ARPA zone. IPv4-only nodes configure only the IPv4 address and IPv6-only nodes only the IPv6 one. It is enough for a single operator to do this, though more operators give more distribution and capacity. Detailed instructions are in RFC 7534.

A zone owner then installs a DNAME record. The RFC's example redirects reverse queries for TEST-NET-1 (192.0.2.0/24) by putting a DNAME in the 192.IN-ADDR.ARPA zone. There is no practical limit to the number of redirections, each can be removed at any time by the owners of that part of the namespace, and no change to AS112 nodes is needed. DNAME records used this way can be signed with DNSSEC.

For continuity, operators should keep answering for the existing three nameservers and the delegation of existing zones should not change. The RFC suggests that once EMPTY.AS112.ARPA is shown to be well hosted, the RFC 1918 zones might move to DNAME redirection, but it gives no such direction to IANA. All zones listed in RFC 6303 are candidates for redirection.
sections.plainLanguage: A zone owner pins up a forwarding sign that points at the helper desk. Taking the sign down later does not bother the helper desk at all.

sections.title: DNAME Support in Resolvers
sections.content:
DNAME was specified years after the original DNS, so not every resolver supports it. RFC 6672 provides a fallback in which the server also sends a synthesised CNAME, and a resolver that does not understand DNAME accepts and caches that CNAME. Re-query frequency follows the TTLs from the authoritative server, and negative caching of the target follows the parameters of the EMPTY.AS112.ARPA zone.

Validating resolvers are required to implement DNAME, so they do not rely on synthesised CNAMEs and the DNAME signature can still be validated. If a recursive server supports DNAME but a stub resolver does not, CNAME synthesis again provides a path. AS112 nodes themselves never need DNAME support.

Appendix A reports an experiment run on 2013-10-10 and 2013-10-11 through an online advertisement, with 338,478 recorded results. At most 1.9% of clients failed to resolve a name with a DNAME redirection, while the control URL failed for 2.8%. The authors conclude there is no evidence of a consistent failure of deployed resolvers to handle DNAME.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old machines do not know what a forwarding sign is, so the sign also comes with a plain note they can read. A big test found that almost everyone could follow the directions.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA assigned the IPv4 block 192.31.196.0/24 (named AS112-v4) and the IPv6 block 2001:4:112::/48 (named AS112-v6), both with an allocation date of 2014-12 and recorded in the special-purpose address registries. Both are marked Source, Destination, Forwardable and Global as True.

IANA hosts and signs the AS112.ARPA zone, which contains the BLACKHOLE host with the two addresses and delegates HOSTNAME and EMPTY to it. The delegation from the ARPA zone follows normal IANA procedure. The IAB approves the delegation of AS112 in the ARPA domain but takes no architectural or technical position on the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The people who hand out internet addresses set aside a street and an address for the helper desk and wrote it in the official book.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it presents no known additional security concerns to the Internet. For the security considerations of AS112 service in general, it refers to RFC 7534. It does note that DNAME records used for redirection can be signed with DNSSEC, which gives a way to authenticate each redirection.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new to worry about here, and the forwarding signs can be stamped so you know they are real.
